steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Latin nouns change their endings to show their grammatical function in a sentence; this system is called declension.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: There are five declensions, each with a characteristic vowel in the stem: 1st (a-stem), 2nd (o-stem), 3rd (consonant/i-stem), 4th (u-stem), 5th (e-stem).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Every Latin noun has a gender: masculine, feminine, or neuter. Gender must be learned with each noun and does not always match natural sex.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: First declension nouns are mostly feminine (e.g. puella, villa, familia). Exceptions like nauta and agricola are masculine.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: How many declensions are there in Latin? | Q: What gender are most first declension nouns? Name two masculine exceptions. | Q: How do you find the stem of a third declension noun?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Five: first (a-stem), second (o-stem), third (consonant/i-stem), fourth (u-stem), and fifth (e-stem). | Mostly feminine. Masculine exceptions include nauta (sailor) and agricola (farmer). | Remove the genitive singular ending (-is) from the genitive form. For example: rex, regis → stem is reg-.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always learn the nominative AND genitive singular of every noun — the genitive is essential for identifying the declension and stem. When translating, identify the noun's case first: the ending tells you its grammatical function in the sentence. Watch for neuter nouns: their nominative and accusative look the same, so context determines which case is meant. Third declension nouns are the most tested — practise recognising i-stems by their genitive plural (-ium) and neuter plural (-ia).
